episodes.title: Episode 06: Three wrong plateaus, and ninety percent
notes: Correction: three stall calls in stage 4 (at ~66%, ~70% and ~79-80% after ~690 flat generations) were each followed by a climb
Real task now: hourly average 84.8% (gens 2382-2522), best check 90% at gen 2462 (200 fresh flights)
Why: 200-flight checks swing several points by luck, and NEAT moves in steps (punctuated equilibrium)
Remaining failures: boulder ~6%, crashes ~6%, off-pad ~1%, timeouts ~1.5%
Training unchanged; a champion must hold 95% on 1,000 fresh selection flights, then two test sets of 1,000
transcript: This episode is a correction, and some good news. Three times since the last episode, I wrote in the log that training had stalled. Three times I was wrong. Let me tell you why that happened, because the reason is one of the most useful ideas in this whole project.

First, the news. At the last episode, the pilot landed about two thirds of the real flights, with full wind and the full boulder. Now, over the last hour, it lands about eighty five out of a hundred. The best single check so far landed ninety percent, at generation two thousand four hundred and sixty two. The goal is ninety five.

Now, the wrong calls. The first time, the checks had sat near seventy percent for about two hundred generations. I called it a stall. In the next hour, they averaged seventy six. The second time was the same story. The third time looked much stronger. For about seven hundred generations, five hours in a row, the average stayed between seventy nine and eighty one. I wrote that a change was needed. Two hours later, the average was eighty five.
Why does this keep happening? There are two reasons, and both are worth understanding.

The first reason is noise. Each check is two hundred flights. Imagine a pilot who truly lands eighty percent. On two hundred flights, it will often score seventy five, or eighty five, just by luck. So a single check tells you little. Even an hour of checks moves around by a few points. If the real gain is one point per hour, you cannot see it from one hour to the next. You need many hours before the trend shows.

The second reason is how evolution itself moves. It does not climb smoothly like a ramp. It moves in steps. For a long time, the population tries small changes, and most do nothing. Then one network finds a new trick. Maybe a new connection that reacts to a gust earlier. That network wins more often, its children spread, and within a hundred generations the whole population has the trick. Then it goes flat again. Biologists have a name for this pattern. They call it punctuated equilibrium. Long calm stretches, then sudden jumps.
Put the two reasons together, and a flat stretch tells you almost nothing about the future. It might be the end. Or it might be the quiet before the next step.

So what is the lesson for me? Calling a plateau is a claim, and it needs evidence. Not one hour, and not even five. And before changing the plan, I should compare against how long the earlier flat stretches lasted. I have added this to the Lessons page.

What are the failures now? About six in a hundred flights touch the boulder. About six crash, mostly in strong gusts. Fewer than two land beside the pad, and fewer than two run out of time. The boulder and the gusts are what's left.

What's next? Training continues unchanged. There are a bit more than four days to the deadline, and at this pace there is real hope for ninety five. When a champion looks good enough, it has to prove it. First on a thousand fresh flights, and then on two separate test sets of a thousand each. I'll be back when that happens, or when something breaks.

episodes.title: Episode 05: Practising the hard cases, and a plateau
notes: Stage 3 (boulder) ended at its 400-generation cap at gen 702 without the 85% pass; boulder at full size since gen 578
Stage 4: the real task with 30% hard cases (flights recent champions failed)
Real-task checks (200 fresh flights): 63.8% avg for gens 702-762, 67.1% for 772-842; best 73.5% (gen 832), best ever 76% (gen 402)
Failures on average: crashes ~13%, boulder ~10%, off-pad ~8%, timeouts ~3.5%
At ~3 points per 100 generations, 95% by Friday needs a change: candidate levers to be measured
transcript: This episode covers the last stretch of the night. The boulder stage ended, the final stage began, and the climb slowed down a lot. Let me explain what happened, and then what it means.

The boulder stage had a simple plan. The rock grows from small to full size as the champion gets better. It reached full size at generation five hundred and seventy eight. But the stage also had a test. It needed eighty five percent on the real task to pass. It never got there. So the stage ended at its time limit, at generation seven hundred and two. Over its last fifty generations, the real task was at about sixty five percent.
Then the final stage began. This is the real task itself, with full wind, full gusts and the full boulder. It adds one new idea, called hard cases.

Here is the idea. Most flights are easy for a good pilot. If every flight counts the same, the easy ones drown out the few that matter. So we keep a list of flights that recent champions failed. About three in ten flights in each generation are taken from that list. A network that learns to handle them gets a clear advantage. Teachers do the same thing. You practise the problems you got wrong, not the ones you already know. In the last project this trick lifted the pilot from about ninety three percent to about ninety six.

So, did it work here? A little. The real task is checked every ten generations, on two hundred fresh flights. In the first sixty generations of this stage, those checks averaged sixty four percent. In the next seventy, sixty seven. The best single check was seventy three and a half percent. The best ever is still seventy six, from much earlier, and that one was probably a lucky draw.

What goes wrong in the failed flights? About thirteen in a hundred are crashes. About ten touch the boulder. About eight land safely, but beside the pad. And three or four run out of time. So it is not one problem. It is several smaller ones, and most of them come from the strong gusts.

Now the honest part. The goal is ninety five percent by Friday. At this pace, about three points per hundred generations, we will not get there. This is what a plateau looks like. Evolution keeps the best networks, but each small improvement is harder to find than the one before. And with only two hundred flights per check, a real gain of two points is hidden in the noise.

There is a second, quieter cause. Each network flies thirty two flights per generation. Two networks of equal skill can differ by several flights just by luck. Evolution then picks the lucky one, not the better one. With more flights per network, or more networks, selection gets cleaner, but each generation costs more time. That is the trade-off at the heart of this method.

So what's next? There are a few levers. More flights per network, so selection is less noisy. A larger share of hard cases. A reward that punishes the specific failures more, like landing beside the pad. Or a bigger population, so there are more ideas to choose from. I'll propose one to you, measured first, rather than guess. Training keeps running in the meantime.

episodes.title: Episode 04: The rock is not the problem
notes: Grid test of the gen-382 champion, 400 analysis flights per cell (results/wind_boulder_grid_g00382_s2_goal.json)
Calm or light wind: ~85-90% landed even with the full boulder; full wind: 73% without boulder, 53% with
The bottleneck is strong gusty wind, not the boulder; a restart from 'small rock, no wind' would re-teach a known skill
Real-task checks on 200 flights swing widely (76% at gen 402, 52% at gen 442): selection uses 1,000 flights
Open question for you: keep stage 3 in full wind, or ramp wind 10 -> 15 together with the boulder
transcript: We are now in the boulder stage. The full wind is on, and the boulder grows from small to full size as the champion improves. You asked a good question. Should the curriculum start over, with a small rock and no wind, then a little wind, and ramp both up as it learns?
It is a sensible plan. Learning one hard thing at a time is a classic curriculum idea. But before changing the plan, I wanted to know where the champion actually fails. So I made a map.

I took the champion from generation three hundred and eighty two. It flew four hundred unseen flights in each of sixteen worlds. Four wind strengths, from calm to full. And four boulders, from none to full size.

Here is what the map said. In calm air, it lands about ninety percent, even with the full boulder. In light wind, about the same. So it already knows how to get past the rock. The weak spot is the full gusty wind. There, with no boulder at all, it lands only seventy three percent. With the full boulder, fifty three. Most of the misses in strong wind are crashes and landings beside the pad. They come from the wind, not the rock.

So restarting with a small rock and no wind would spend hours teaching a skill it already has. That is the main lesson here. Measure where the learner fails before you change the lessons. A map like this costs a few minutes, and it can save hours.

Your idea is still right in one way. Raising both difficulties together, paced by success, is a good design. The open question is where to start. One option keeps going as now, in full wind. The other starts the rock stage at a medium wind, where the champion lands about eighty percent, and grows wind and rock together. It is easier to keep a learner moving when it is succeeding.

There is a reason this matters. The pace rule only speeds up when the champion lands seven flights out of ten. In full wind the champion hovers right around that line, so the rock often grows at half speed. In about a hundred and fifty generations, the rock went from forty percent to almost seventy percent of full size.

One more thing to learn from the numbers. Every ten generations, the champion flies two hundred fresh flights of the real task. Those results jump around a lot. Generation four hundred and two landed seventy six percent. Forty generations later, a different champion landed fifty two. Some of that is real, but much of it is luck. Two hundred flights is a small sample. And the champion is picked as the best of many, so it often looks better than it really is. This is called the winner's curse. That is why the final choice of champion uses a thousand flights, and the goal test two separate thousands.

What's next? I'll keep watching the run and update the site as it goes. When you decide about the rock stage, I'll make the change at the next generation and log it, without losing the population. Either way, the real test comes when the rock is at full size.

episodes.title: Episode 03: Five times faster, and why not ten
notes: Wall clock per generation: ~101 s -> ~19 s (about 5.3x)
numba network: 46 -> 5 microseconds per decision; C++ flights: 95 -> 18 s of flying per generation
C++ sim is bit-identical to a fresh reference env on 3,000 of 3,000 flights; checks and the goal test still fly the reference
NEAT crossover and distance rewritten (same results): ~6 s -> ~1.5 s per generation
Workers measured: 4 -> 22.8 s, 8 -> 18.9 s per generation; 8 is the default now
transcript: This episode is about speed. In evolution, speed is everything. Every generation, three hundred networks each fly twenty four flights. That is about two million small physics steps. The faster we fly, the more generations fit before Friday.
This morning, one generation took about a hundred seconds. Now it takes about nineteen. That is a bit more than five times faster. Here is how, and what it teaches.

The first rule of speed work is to measure before you change anything. Where does the time go? I timed every part of one flight step. Some went to the physics. A lot went to Python itself. Python is easy to write, but every small operation has overhead. Our simulator wraps the physics in several layers, and each layer costs a little on every step.

Step one was the network. Every step, the network reads sixteen numbers and picks one of four actions. I compiled that part to machine code with a tool called numba. One decision went from forty six millionths of a second to five. Step two was a lean copy of the flight code, without the layers. Together, a generation went from ninety five seconds of flying to forty eight.

Step three was the big one. I rewrote the whole flight in C plus plus. It uses the very same physics engine, compiled from the same source code. One call now flies a whole batch of flights with no Python in the loop. Flying time dropped to eighteen seconds.

But a faster simulator is only useful if it is the same simulator. If it differs, evolution learns the wrong world. So I tested it. The same network flew the same thousand flights in both versions, in three different worlds. Three thousand of three thousand flights matched bit for bit, every position and every number. Even so, the rules stay strict. The fast version is only for training. Every check, every choice of champion and the final test still fly the original.

That test found something surprising. The original simulator does not always agree with itself. If you reuse it for many flights, the last digits can differ after touchdown. The physics engine recycles the internal numbers of deleted objects, and that changes the order of tiny sums. It almost never changes an outcome, but it is a good reminder. Exact repeatability is something you have to test, not assume.

Then a new surprise. With flying at eighteen seconds, a generation still took twenty seven. The other nine went to the evolution library itself, while all workers sat idle. Making children was slow. For every gene a child inherits, the library checked the whole network for loops, again and again. I rewrote that check and the distance between networks with the same logic. Same children, same species, four and a half times faster. This is a classic pattern. Speed up the biggest part, and the second biggest part becomes the new wall.

Last, the number of workers. The laptop has four real cores, and each can run two threads. I measured four, five, six, seven and eight workers on the same generations. Eight was best, but only seventeen percent faster than four. Two threads on one core share the same machinery, so the second thread adds little.

Why not ten times, as planned? Because the physics engine itself is the floor. This game asks it to solve every step with a hundred and eighty passes for speed and sixty for position. That work is the same in any language. Making it cheaper would mean changing the physics, and then we would be learning a different game. So we stop at five.

episodes.title: Episode 02: Species, wind, and a correction
notes: Correction to episode 1: species collapsed because a resumed run kept an old threshold of 46.8, not because of the threshold floor
Threshold chosen by simulation on the saved population: 0.3 gave 79 species, 0.4 gave 13
Gen 211 diagnosis: 97.5% in its practice world, 67% in full wind, 0% with a boulder in calm air
Paced ramps from gen 230: 3x speed at >= 90% landed, 1x at >= 70%, 0.5x below
Stage 2 (wind) passed at gen 301: 87.5% of 200 fresh full-wind flights
transcript: Welcome back. In the first episode, evolution learned to land in calm air. This one covers the wind stage. It also covers a mistake I told you about wrongly last time, so let me start there.

First, a quick idea you need. In this method, every network belongs to a species. A species is a group of networks that are built alike. Networks only compete hard inside their own species. Why does that matter? A new neuron usually makes a network worse at first. Its weights are still random. Without protection, that network dies before the new neuron becomes useful. Species give new ideas a few generations of shelter. So the number of species is a health sign. Too few, and new ideas die. Too many, and each group is too small to improve.

To decide who belongs together, the method measures a distance between two networks. It counts the genes they do not share, and how different the shared weights are. If the distance is below a threshold, they share a species.

In the last episode I said the species had collapsed to three because my lower limit on the threshold was too high. That was wrong. I lowered the limit and nothing changed. So I measured instead of guessing. Members of each species sat far from each other. Far more than the threshold allowed. That was impossible, unless the threshold in use was not the one I was setting. And that was the bug. When the run restarted from a saved file, the part that sorts species loaded its own old copy of the settings. It kept a runaway value of forty six from an early restart. My controller had been tuning a number that nobody read. For a hundred and forty generations, everything was lumped into old species until only three were left.
The lesson is general. When you save and resume a program, check that the resumed program really uses the live settings. Now a test checks exactly that.

The fix caused one more problem. With the real threshold back, my first choice split the population into a hundred and five species. Each species needs at least three members. A hundred and five times three is more than three hundred, so the program stopped. This time I chose by measurement. I sorted the saved population with different thresholds and counted the species. Zero point four gave thirteen. That is what the run uses now.

Now the wind. The wind grew slowly, from a soft steady push to the full gusty wind with turbulence. At generation two hundred and eleven I checked the champion in different worlds. In its own practice world, it landed ninety seven and a half percent. In full wind, sixty seven percent. That was up from fifteen percent at the start of the stage. So wind learning worked. But with the boulder, even in calm air, it landed zero percent. It had simply never met the boulder.

That check also showed a second problem. The wind grew on a fixed clock. The champion was landing almost every flight, and still had to wait. A good teacher does not wait when the student is bored. So I made the ramp follow the student. When the champion lands nine flights out of ten, the wind grows three times faster. Between seven and nine, normal speed. Below seven, half speed. This idea is called pacing. You keep the learner at the edge of what it can do. Not so easy that time is wasted, and not so hard that it fails every time.
I also mixed a small boulder into a quarter of the wind flights, so the route skill could start early.

It worked. At generation three hundred and one, the wind stage passed. The champion landed eighty seven and a half percent of two hundred fresh flights in full wind, with no boulder. Then the boulder stage began. That is the next story, together with a big speed-up.

episodes.title: Episode 01: Evolution starts from nothing
notes: Goal set by you: NEAT from random networks, >= 95% landed on 1,000 unseen flights, by Fri 6 Nov 17:00
Boulder layout v3: always >= 3.5 m of free air above and below; the PPO champion lands 98.9% on it
Size test: copies of the PPO pilot land 56.5% (8 hidden), 79.1% (16), 87.0% (32), so NEAT starts with 32 hidden neurons
Stage 1 (calm landing) passed at generation 100: 96.5% and 97.5% on two fresh sets of 200
Two speciation bugs found and fixed (threshold ran 0.25 -> 46.8; then species fell to 3); the run resumed from its checkpoint
transcript: This is the first episode of the new lander project. You asked for something bold. No copied pilot this time, and no head start. Just evolution, from random networks, until the lander touches down safely in ninety five out of a hundred unseen flights. The deadline is Friday at five in the afternoon.

Let me remind you of the task. The lander flies in strong, gusty wind with turbulence on top. A boulder floats in the air on the way down. The pilot cannot see the wind. It only sees sixteen numbers, like its position, its speed, and its own estimate of the wind.

Before anything else, I made the world fairer. In the old layout, the boulder could hang less than two metres above the landing pad. The lander itself is almost two metres tall. So sometimes the only way in was a gap smaller than the ship. Now the boulder always leaves at least three and a half metres of free air below it, and the same above it. A test checks this on six hundred thousand layouts. On this fairer world, last project's champion lands ninety eight point nine percent of a thousand fresh flights. That is the bar.

Next I asked a simple question. How big must the brain be? I copied the old champion into small networks and let each one fly a thousand times. With eight hidden neurons, the copy landed only fifty six percent. With sixteen, seventy nine percent. With thirty two, eighty seven percent. So a small brain is not enough. These copies were only a ruler. None of them is used for evolution.

So here is the setup. Three hundred random networks. Each starts with thirty two hidden neurons and six hundred and forty connections, all with random weights. Every generation, each network flies the same flights, so the weather is fair to everyone. The best ones have children. Children get small changes to their weights. Sometimes a neuron or a connection is added. And, as you asked, sometimes one is removed.

The curriculum has four steps. First, calm air with training wheels, a gentle force that keeps the lander upright and slowly fades away. Then the wind grows from soft to full strength. Then the boulder grows from small to full size. And finally the real task, with extra practice on the flights it failed.

The first step went well. In the first generation, the average network scored minus three hundred and forty two. That means almost every one crashed. By generation eighteen, the best network landed every one of its calm practice flights. At generation one hundred, with the training wheels gone, it passed the test. It landed ninety six and a half percent of two hundred fresh calm flights, and ninety seven and a half percent on a second fresh set.

Now the failures. I made two mistakes in the part that sorts networks into species. Species matter in this method. They protect a new idea, like a fresh neuron, while it is still clumsy. First, my controller kept raising the bar for what counts as a new species. It went from a quarter to above forty, while the number of species never moved. No new species could ever have formed. I caught it at generation fifty four, capped it, and resumed the run from its checkpoint. Then, a hundred generations later, the cap itself was the problem. The population had shrunk to three species of exactly one hundred each, three tight family lines. So I lowered the floor. Nothing was lost either time, but I want you to know the numbers came from a bumpy road.

What's next? The wind is now at about half strength and still mostly steady. Over the next two hundred generations it becomes the full gusty wind with turbulence. On the real task, with wind and the boulder, the best network so far lands only six percent. That is expected. It has never met the boulder. Each generation now takes about a minute and a half. I'll be back when the wind stage is passed, or when something breaks.
